crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR data is a set of guiding principles for research data: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make datasets, papers, models and tools findable, comparable and reusable.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers methods for research institutions to jointly analyze or train models on restricted datasets without moving raw records to a central repository.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organization's entities, documents, people, projects, datasets, and their relationships, maintained by a university, library, or research institute.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation is the set of policies, technologies and practices that keep research data and repository objects readable, usable and authentic for decades or longer.

sections.body: Research data and repositories is the part of artificial intelligence work that treats datasets, metadata, and archives as first class objects rather than as raw inputs. In practice, AI systems now extract metadata from papers and reports, align terms across ontologies, resolve duplicate author and institution names, and build links between datasets, code, and publications. They also help classify sensitive records, suggest access controls, and generate summaries that make a repository easier to search. Federated methods let several institutions train models or run queries without pooling identifiable data in one place. The site's own library holds 135 research papers, and the same pattern appears there, where extracted claims and glossary terms depend on careful metadata work. The aim is not to replace curators but to reduce the manual effort that has always limited how much data can be described and reused.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are settled. Basic metadata extraction, citation parsing, and search over well structured records work reliably enough for daily use, and knowledge graphs built from clean institutional sources can answer real questions. Other parts remain hard. Semantic interoperability across disciplines is still fragile because ontologies encode local assumptions, and automated mappings often need expert review. Federated sharing of sensitive data runs into legal, ethical, and technical friction that no model solves on its own, and privacy guarantees can be difficult to verify in practice. Long term preservation is never finished, because formats, software, and hardware change, and a preserved object must remain usable, not merely stored. The honest limit is that AI can accelerate description, linking, and monitoring, but it cannot decide what deserves to be kept or guarantee that a complex digital object will still run decades from now.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section form a chain from principles to practice. FAIR Data sets out the findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable expectations that shape repository work. Metadata and Ontologies explains the vocabularies and schemas that make those expectations operational, and it is the place to go for questions about terms, identifiers, and mappings. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data covers the methods and governance needed when records cannot be centralized, which matters for health, finance, and other protected domains. The page on Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows how an organization can connect its own people, projects, datasets, and outputs into a queryable whole. Long Term Digital Preservation closes the chain by asking how all of this survives format change, bit rot, and the retirement of the software that created it.
